qtr.text: In words of two syllables the stress falls almost always on the first syllable. In words of three syllables, on the first or else on the middle syllable. 5267.prule: Word stress is predominantly initial: disyllables are almost always stressed on the first syllable; four-syllable words usually carry accents on the first and third syllables (alternating rhythm; which of the two carries the main accent is marked per item — e.g. o e moerinam 'index finger' on the first, atem i e rim 'middle finger' on the third — not stated as a rule); trisyllables vary between initial and second-syllable (medial) stress, item by item. 5284.prule: In the 18th-century Tarahumara recorded by Steffel (mostly Tomochic district, 1763-65), word stress is lexically contrastive and not predictable (minimal pairs guacá/guáca, hulí/húli), but confined to an initial three-syllable window: 97% of 1086 reliably accented words carry one stress on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd syllable (9% / 60% / 28%); disyllables are 94% final(=2nd)-stressed, trisyllables split 42% second vs 47% third, 4-syllable words 72% second. This matches the initial three-syllable stress window described for modern Rarámuri varieties (Choguita, Norogachi).
5284.srule: Merrill: about 2% of words are written with two accents (compounds written as one word with an accent on each member, words in progressive -simí, and some 5-6-syllable words on 2nd+4th; words in -rúgame ~ -túgame, -guí, locative -tschíc and interrogative -tsá instead carry a single accent that may fall on the 4th syllable); 'es imposible determinar si el doble acento representaba dos acentos de la misma intensidad o el acento primario y secundario' (p.730). Steffel's acute vs grave accent difference is typographical, not primary/secondary (ch.7.3 p.452).

qtr.text: Nisupu [Nyisuphu] is the name of a small branch within the Yi nationality. The most salient features of Nisu [Nyisu] Yi are that it has many consonants and few vowels, and a tense/lax vowel opposition. There are 3 tones, and tense and lax vowels both occur under every tone. Nisu Yi still preserves a complete set of lateral-release stops tl, tlh, dl, ndlh. This set of sounds corresponds regularly across all the major Yi dialects.
